Pregnancy

Coconut oil in pregnancy: uses, evidence and limits

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Coconut oil is often presented as one product with dozens of pregnancy benefits. Some uses are ordinary food or personal-care choices; others rely on small studies or claims that have not been established. Knowing the difference helps you choose a useful product without overlooking a symptom that needs care.

Food, skin care and treatment are different questions

Coconut oil is used for cooking, moisturising, hair care and a variety of home remedies. Being edible does not prove that it treats a medical condition or that every way of applying it is suitable during pregnancy. A small amount in a recipe, an ingredient in a skin product and an intravaginal remedy need different considerations.

The useful question is what you want it to do. Adding flavour is different from treating eczema, preventing a tear at birth or stopping haemorrhoid pain. If a symptom needs assessment, trying a familiar household product should not delay that assessment.

What coconut oil contributes to a diet

Coconut oil is almost entirely fat, with roughly 80–90 percent of that fat saturated. Lauric acid makes up a large share. It is energy dense and provides little of the fibre, protein or micronutrient variety found in whole foods. Check the label for the serving size and fat content of the product you use.

Fat is part of a balanced pregnancy diet, but coconut oil has not been shown to be necessary for placental development or a baby’s organs. Olive, canola and other suitable liquid oils generally provide more unsaturated fat. Coconut oil should not be described as nutritionally equivalent to those oils simply because all are plant-derived.

Ordinary coconut oil is not the same as purified MCT oil

Claims about rapid energy use and less fat storage often come from research on specially prepared medium-chain triglyceride oils. Commercial coconut oil has a different fatty-acid mixture. Lauric acid has twelve carbon atoms and does not behave in the body exactly like the shorter fatty acids used in many purified MCT products.

You cannot therefore assume that coconut oil goes straight to the liver, is never stored as body fat or has a proven pregnancy weight-management benefit. Nor does a review of fat metabolism establish a safe or useful daily supplement dose for pregnancy. Treat a cooking oil as a food ingredient rather than a metabolic treatment.

Use it for flavour without adding a daily oil supplement

If you like its taste and tolerate it, a modest amount can be part of a cooked dish, such as vegetables or a sauce. Adding spoonfuls to every smoothie, eating it directly or replacing all other fats is unnecessary. The overall pattern of food and the balance of saturated and unsaturated fats matter more than one fashionable ingredient.

Virgin oil is processed differently from refined oil and often has a stronger coconut flavour. Those terms do not demonstrate superior pregnancy outcomes or make a product medicinal. Check ingredients if using a cosmetic blend, avoid anything you are allergic to, and follow ordinary storage and food-hygiene instructions.

Oil pulling has limited evidence

Oil pulling means swishing an edible oil around the mouth and spitting it out. Traditional descriptions often use a spoonful for up to twenty minutes, sometimes before breakfast. That describes the practice; it is not an established pregnancy dental prescription.

A 2016 systematic review included five small trials with 160 participants, lasting only ten to forty-five days. Some short-term findings were encouraging, but study quality varied and several comparisons showed no significant difference from controls. These results do not prove prevention of cavities or general health benefits. Claims about treating migraine, allergies or kidney problems, or strengthening mouth muscles, lack adequate clinical support.

Protect your teeth and gums during pregnancy

Hormonal changes can make gums more prone to inflammation, and repeated vomiting can expose teeth to stomach acid. Those are reasons for routine dental care, not reasons to substitute oil for it. Brush with fluoride toothpaste, clean between teeth and discuss persistent bleeding, pain or vomiting-related problems with your dentist.

The American Dental Association does not recommend oil pulling as a dental-hygiene method. Prolonged swishing may also be unpleasant with nausea; do not gargle or deliberately swallow the oil. If someone chooses to try it, spitting it into the bin avoids putting oil down the drain, but that practical detail does not make it an effective treatment. Necessary dental care can be provided during pregnancy.

Moisturising and eczema: possible comfort, limited pregnancy evidence

Coconut oil can reduce a dry feeling for some people, but it may irritate others. Eczema can first appear or flare during pregnancy, and treatment should reflect severity and the body site. A 2007 clinical review discusses this pregnancy context; it does not establish coconut oil as the preferred treatment.

A randomised study of 117 children with mild to moderate atopic dermatitis found improvement with virgin coconut oil over eight weeks compared with mineral oil. This is evidence in children, not a trial proving treatment effectiveness or safety for every pregnant person. Ask about an appropriate moisturiser and any needed prescribed treatment instead of stopping an effective eczema plan.

Laboratory skin findings do not establish a home remedy

Research published in a 2019 journal issue examined virgin coconut oil in cell and reconstructed-skin models. It reported changes in inflammatory markers and barrier-related proteins. These are laboratory findings, not evidence that applying kitchen oil will cure an inflammatory skin disease during pregnancy.

A 2017 review of plant oils also discusses antioxidant effects, wound repair and skin-barrier mechanisms. Findings involving collagen or microbial growth do not prove that coconut oil can safely disinfect a wound, replace a dressing or treat an infection. Do not apply it to a surgical wound or a suspected infection unless your clinical team specifically recommends the product.

Stretch marks are not a sign that you missed a treatment

Stretch marks can develop on the abdomen, thighs, buttocks, breasts or upper arms as skin changes. Their appearance varies with skin tone and often becomes less noticeable over time. A moisturiser may improve comfort when the skin feels dry, but it cannot promise to prevent marks or erase them.

Evidence that an oil affects skin cells or wound collagen cannot be transferred directly to stretch-mark prevention. NHS information describes limited evidence for oils and creams preventing them. There is no need to spend money on a coconut-oil routine out of fear that ordinary pregnancy skin changes are your fault.

Do not assume all pregnancy itching is dry skin

Ask your maternity team about persistent itching, especially if it is severe at night or affects the palms or soles. Itching can have causes that need investigation, including intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy. A soothing product making the skin feel better does not rule those conditions out.

A new rash, swelling, painful skin, oozing or signs of infection also deserves advice. For an ordinary dry patch, introduce any new product cautiously and stop if it stings or causes a rash. A small-area trial cannot guarantee that an allergy will never occur, and known coconut allergy is a reason to avoid it.

Perineal massage is about technique and timing, not a special oil

The perineum is the tissue between the vaginal opening and anus. Antenatal perineal massage may reduce some birth trauma, particularly before a first vaginal birth, but it cannot guarantee that tearing will be avoided. RCOG describes starting from 35 weeks; some local services use 34 weeks. Ask your midwife which approach fits your pregnancy.

With clean hands, short nails and a comfortable supported position, a clinician-approved technique uses gentle downward and sideways pressure followed by a U-shaped movement along the lower vaginal opening. A stretching sensation should not become sharp pain. Ask for a demonstration or written instructions about duration and frequency rather than forcing a fixed depth or repeating a painful routine.

Check when massage and intimate use are unsuitable

Do not perform perineal massage if your waters may have broken or you have thrush, herpes or another vaginal infection. Ask first if you have bleeding, have been told to avoid vaginal penetration or have another pregnancy complication. Use a lubricant recommended by your maternity team and avoid ingredients that cause allergy or irritation.

A product being suggested for late-pregnancy massage does not establish that routine intravaginal use prevents yeast infections or treats dryness. Coconut oil is not a proven treatment for thrush. For sexual comfort, choose a suitable personal lubricant and check compatibility: oils can damage latex and polyisoprene condoms. Water-based or compatible silicone-based products are usually more straightforward; follow the product instructions.

Hair conditioning is different from treating hair loss

A 2003 laboratory hair-care study compared coconut, mineral and sunflower oils. Coconut oil reduced protein loss from damaged and undamaged hair in the conditions studied, when used before or after washing. The work supports a possible conditioning role, not a claim that it stimulates new hair growth or prevents hormonal shedding.

If you enjoy using it, try a small amount on the hair lengths and wash it out as needed. Avoid hot oil and stop if the scalp becomes irritated. The study was conducted by researchers affiliated with a hair-product manufacturer and was not a pregnancy trial. Sudden, patchy or troublesome hair loss deserves assessment rather than repeated oil treatments.

A small haemorrhoid trial is a starting point, not a prescription

One small randomised study conducted in 2019 involved sixty pregnant women with haemorrhoids. It compared a coconut-oil ointment regimen over two weeks with a control group; both groups received lifestyle advice. The authors reported improved pain, itching, prolapse and overall symptom scores in the ointment group.

A single small, short study cannot establish broad safety, long-term effectiveness or the best formulation. It also does not show that eating coconut oil helps or that kitchen oil is equivalent to the studied ointment. Ask your midwife, pharmacist or clinician about appropriate treatment rather than copying an applicator regimen from a study description.

For piles, keep stools comfortable and check bleeding

Haemorrhoids can cause soreness, itching, swelling or bright-red bleeding after a bowel movement. Adequate fibre and fluids, regular movement and avoiding straining can help when constipation contributes. A low-fibre diet is not the recommended strategy. Gentle cleaning and a cool cloth may improve comfort.

Ask before using a haemorrhoid product during pregnancy, and have new or unexplained rectal bleeding assessed. Severe pain, heavy bleeding or feeling unwell needs prompt care. An ointment may ease a symptom without correcting constipation or another cause of pain, so a treatment plan should address both.

Recognise irritation, allergy and emergency symptoms

Stop using the product if you develop itching, hives, a new rash, stomach upset or other symptoms that appear linked to it, and seek advice. Nasal or eye symptoms can occur with allergies, but a headache alone is not specific evidence of coconut allergy. Do not keep testing a product after a suspected reaction.

Wheezing, chest tightness, breathing difficulty, swelling of the tongue or throat, marked dizziness or collapse can indicate a severe allergic reaction. Call emergency services and use prescribed adrenaline if your allergy plan tells you to do so. These are not minor side effects to watch at home. Tell the maternity team what happened and keep the product details for assessment.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Evidence must be separated by use: eating an oil, conditioning hair, applying it to skin and using an ointment in a trial are not interchangeable.

Laboratory findings and small trials do not establish broad pregnancy treatment benefits or a home-treatment dose.

How BeMama can help

Start with the symptom or purpose, then check whether the product and route of use fit the evidence and your pregnancy care plan.

When to seek help

Obstetric, dietetic, dental and dermatology review remain pending. No intravaginal remedy, supplement dose or haemorrhoid applicator regimen is prescribed.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Coconut oil is high in saturated fat and is not equivalent to purified MCT oil.
  • It cannot replace dental care, eczema treatment or evaluation of pregnancy itching.
  • Stretch-mark prevention and hair-growth claims are not established.
  • Perineal massage and haemorrhoid treatment need appropriate guidance.

Frequently asked questions

Can I cook with coconut oil during pregnancy?

A modest amount can be an ordinary food choice if you tolerate it. It is not a required supplement, and unsaturated oils are generally preferable for much of your cooking.

Is it the same as MCT oil?

No. The fatty-acid mixture differs, so findings from purified MCT products cannot be applied directly to ordinary coconut oil.

Can oil pulling replace brushing or dental treatment?

No. Use fluoride toothpaste and interdental cleaning, and seek dental care for symptoms. The ADA does not recommend oil pulling for dental hygiene.

Does the eczema research prove it works in pregnancy?

No. A paediatric trial and laboratory skin studies do not establish a universal pregnancy treatment.

Will rubbing it on my abdomen prevent stretch marks?

That benefit is not established. Moisturising may ease dryness, but stretch marks are not evidence that you neglected your skin.

Can I use it to ignore itching on my palms or soles?

No. Contact your maternity team about that pattern of itching, even if a moisturiser temporarily helps.

When can perineal massage begin?

RCOG describes starting from 35 weeks. Confirm timing and suitability with your maternity team, especially if you have complications.

Is coconut oil compatible with condoms?

It can damage latex and polyisoprene condoms. Use a lubricant that the condom manufacturer says is compatible.

Does the haemorrhoid study justify a home coconut-oil treatment?

No. It was a small, short ointment trial, not proof that kitchen oil or oral coconut oil is an effective or safe substitute.

Is wheezing after using it a mild allergy symptom?

No. Wheezing, throat swelling, breathing difficulty or collapse can be an emergency. Follow your allergy plan and call emergency services.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
